author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: A 1967 Cold War satire in which the superpowers' rival weapons designers secretly produce useless 'pluriforms'—elaborate fake armaments to reassure their populations—until a genuine alien invasion forces the two frauds to build a weapon that actually works.
page_summary:
In a world locked in an arms race, the weapons of East and West are designed by trance-channeling 'weapons fashion designers' like Lars Powderdry, who produce impressive but functionally useless armaments that are paraded to keep the public feeling defended. The whole military-industrial spectacle is an agreed-upon sham, a theater of deterrence in which nothing built is meant to fire. When an actual alien threat arrives, the two rival designers, who have been faking their entire careers, must collaborate to invent a weapon that can genuinely repel it.

The novel is broad satire aimed at the Cold War economy of appearances: security as performance, weapons as propaganda props, and expertise as elaborate fakery sustained because both sides prefer the show to the truth. Dick lampoons the way a whole civilization can organize itself around a comforting illusion, and then puts that illusion to the test of a real emergency it is wholly unequipped to meet.

Developed from the earlier story 'Project Plowshare' and published by Pyramid in 1967, The Zap Gun is a minor, deliberately absurdist entry, valued for its sardonic take on the arms race rather than for metaphysical depth.
